frontHtml: Identify the HBV replication step targeted by nucleos(t)ide analogues and explain why therapy is long-term.
backHtml: HBV nucleos(t)ide analogues inhibit reverse transcription; they suppress but rarely eradicate infection because cccDNA persists.

frontHtml: Explain the dependence of hepatitis D virus on HBV surface antigen.
backHtml: HDV needs HBsAg for its coat; HBV vaccination therefore also prevents HDV.

frontHtml: Recognise hepatitis E as a cause of fulminant hepatitis in pregnancy.
backHtml: Waterborne hepatitis in a pregnant traveller with negative HAV, HBV and HCV tests suggests HEV, which can be fulminant in pregnancy.

frontHtml: Link incubation period and food vehicle to a preformed-toxin food poisoning.
backHtml: Vomiting within hours of reheated rice points to the preformed emetic toxin of B. cereus.

frontHtml: Describe the molecular action of C. difficile toxins and the resulting pathology.
backHtml: C. difficile toxins inactivate Rho GTPases; the tissue result is pseudomembranous colitis.

frontHtml: Recognise the clinical pattern and microscopic appearance of giardiasis.
backHtml: Noninvasive steatorrheic diarrhea after stream water suggests Giardia, seen as binucleate flagellated trophozoites.

frontHtml: Identify the histopathology of amebic colitis.
backHtml: Amebic colitis shows flask-shaped ulcers with erythrophagocytic trophozoites.

frontHtml: Distinguish Whipple disease from MAC enteritis on biopsy.
backHtml: PAS-positive, acid-fast-negative foamy macrophages in the small bowel of a middle-aged man with arthralgia and cognitive change indicate Whipple disease.

frontHtml: Explain the virulence factor that allows H. pylori to colonise the stomach.
backHtml: H. pylori survives gastric acid through urease-generated ammonia; the same enzyme underlies its diagnostic tests.

frontHtml: Interpret a hepatitis B serologic panel showing the window period.
backHtml: HBsAg negative, anti-HBs negative and IgM anti-HBc positive equals the window period of acute HBV.

frontHtml: Choose first-line therapy for chronic hepatitis C.
backHtml: Chronic HCV is cured with short pangenotypic DAA regimens such as sofosbuvir-velpatasvir.

frontHtml: Select first-line therapy for an initial episode of C. difficile infection.
backHtml: First-episode C. difficile infection is treated with oral fidaxomicin (or oral vancomycin), not metronidazole.

frontHtml: Differentiate amebic from pyogenic liver abscess on clinical grounds.
backHtml: A solitary right-lobe abscess after time in an endemic area, without biliary disease, suggests amebic abscess even without diarrhea.

frontHtml: Treat amebic liver abscess with tissue and luminal agents.
backHtml: Amebic liver abscess is treated medically with metronidazole and then a luminal agent; drainage is the exception.

frontHtml: Select and time the appropriate test of cure after H. pylori therapy.
backHtml: Confirm H. pylori eradication with a breath or stool antigen test 4 or more weeks after therapy and 2 weeks off PPIs.

frontHtml: Manage Shiga toxin-producing E. coli infection in a child.
backHtml: In suspected STEC infection give fluids and monitor for HUS; avoid antibiotics and antimotility drugs.

frontHtml: Manage hepatic echinococcal cyst.
backHtml: Hydatid cysts are treated with albendazole plus procedural management; avoid unprotected aspiration.

frontHtml: Choose post-exposure prophylaxis for hepatitis A.
backHtml: Healthy household contacts of hepatitis A receive hepatitis A vaccine within 2 weeks of exposure.

frontHtml: Recognise the histopathology of Crohn disease.
backHtml: Crohn disease is transmural with noncaseating granulomas; UC is mucosal with crypt abscesses.

frontHtml: Associate primary sclerosing cholangitis with cholangiocarcinoma.
backHtml: PSC in a patient with UC carries a major risk of cholangiocarcinoma.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of vedolizumab and contrast it with natalizumab.
backHtml: Vedolizumab is gut-selective anti-alpha4beta7 therapy; natalizumab is the non-selective alpha4 antibody with PML risk.

frontHtml: Explain the pharmacogenetic basis of thiopurine toxicity.
backHtml: Check TPMT (and NUDT15) before thiopurines; low activity causes severe myelosuppression.

frontHtml: Explain the role of tissue transglutaminase in celiac disease pathogenesis.
backHtml: In celiac disease tTG deamidates gliadin, enhancing DQ2/DQ8 presentation to T cells.

frontHtml: Identify the immunofluorescence pattern of dermatitis herpetiformis.
backHtml: Dermatitis herpetiformis shows granular IgA in dermal papillae and signals celiac disease.

frontHtml: Recognise the histology of collagenous colitis and its drug triggers.
backHtml: Microscopic colitis is diagnosed only on biopsy; collagenous colitis shows a thickened subepithelial collagen band.

frontHtml: Explain the immunopathogenesis of eosinophilic esophagitis.
backHtml: EoE is a Th2 allergic disease of the esophagus mediated by IL-5 and IL-13.

frontHtml: Predict gastric acid and gastrin levels in autoimmune gastritis.
backHtml: Autoimmune gastritis produces achlorhydria with high gastrin and B12 deficiency.

frontHtml: Interpret celiac serology in the setting of selective IgA deficiency.
backHtml: Always measure total IgA with tTG-IgA; if IgA is deficient, use IgG-based celiac serology.

frontHtml: Recognise acute severe ulcerative colitis and start first-line therapy.
backHtml: Acute severe UC is treated first with IV corticosteroids in hospital.

frontHtml: Choose rescue therapy for steroid-refractory acute severe UC.
backHtml: Steroid-refractory acute severe UC is rescued with infliximab or cyclosporine, or treated with colectomy.

frontHtml: Apply colorectal cancer surveillance rules for IBD with PSC.
backHtml: IBD plus PSC means surveillance colonoscopy from PSC diagnosis and every year thereafter.

frontHtml: Manage perianal fistulizing Crohn disease.
backHtml: After draining any abscess, perianal fistulizing Crohn disease is treated with an anti-TNF such as infliximab.

frontHtml: Treat autoimmune hepatitis.
backHtml: Autoimmune hepatitis is treated with corticosteroids plus azathioprine.

frontHtml: Choose initial therapy for eosinophilic esophagitis.
backHtml: EoE is treated first with a PPI, swallowed topical steroids or diet elimination; procedures for motility disorders have no role.

frontHtml: Identify required safety screening before anti-TNF therapy.
backHtml: Screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B before starting anti-TNF therapy.

frontHtml: Treat microscopic colitis.
backHtml: Budesonide is first-line therapy for microscopic colitis once culprit drugs are removed.

frontHtml: Link villous adenoma to secretory diarrhea and hypokalemia.
backHtml: A large rectal villous adenoma can cause mucous diarrhea with hypokalemia.

frontHtml: Identify the molecular initiation of the serrated pathway.
backHtml: Sessile serrated lesions start with BRAF mutation and progress through CpG island methylation and MLH1 silencing.

frontHtml: Describe the function of APC and its role in FAP.
backHtml: APC normally degrades beta-catenin; its germline loss causes FAP.

frontHtml: Recognise the histology and features of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome.
backHtml: Peutz-Jeghers polyps are hamartomas with arborizing smooth muscle; think STK11.

frontHtml: Identify hepatic adenoma as a cause of intraperitoneal hemorrhage.
backHtml: A bleeding hypervascular liver mass in a woman on long-term oral contraceptives suggests hepatic adenoma.

frontHtml: Explain the pathogenesis of focal nodular hyperplasia.
backHtml: FNH is a polyclonal hyperplastic reaction to an abnormal artery, seen as a nodule with a central stellate scar.

frontHtml: Recognise the pathology of serous cystadenoma of the pancreas.
backHtml: Serous cystadenoma is microcystic, glycogen-rich and benign.

frontHtml: Use immunohistochemistry to separate leiomyoma from GIST.
backHtml: Esophageal leiomyoma is desmin positive and KIT/DOG1 negative, unlike GIST.

frontHtml: Associate juvenile polyposis and HHT with SMAD4.
backHtml: Juvenile polyposis with features of HHT points to SMAD4.

frontHtml: Apply post-polypectomy surveillance intervals to an advanced adenoma.
backHtml: Any adenoma 10 mm or larger means surveillance colonoscopy in 3 years.

frontHtml: Avoid over-surveillance after removal of small hyperplastic polyps.
backHtml: Small hyperplastic polyps only: next colonoscopy in 10 years.

frontHtml: Choose the imaging test to characterise an incidental liver mass.
backHtml: Characterise an incidental liver mass with multiphase MRI before considering biopsy or surgery.

frontHtml: Manage a persistent large hepatocellular adenoma.
backHtml: A hepatic adenoma persisting at 5 cm or larger after stopping estrogen should be resected.

frontHtml: Diagnose focal nodular hyperplasia from MRI features.
backHtml: A homogeneously enhancing lesion with a T2-bright central scar and hepatobiliary contrast retention is FNH.

frontHtml: Manage a pancreatic cyst with worrisome features.
backHtml: Pancreatic cysts with worrisome features need EUS with FNA; high-risk stigmata need surgery.

frontHtml: Distinguish a pancreatic pseudocyst from cystic neoplasms.
backHtml: A collection after pancreatitis with very high fluid amylase and low CEA is a pseudocyst.

frontHtml: Choose the surgical approach in familial adenomatous polyposis.
backHtml: FAP with a heavy rectal burden is treated with proctocolectomy and an ileal pouch; duodenal surveillance continues afterwards.

frontHtml: Apply follow-up guidance after piecemeal polypectomy.
backHtml: After piecemeal removal of a lesion 20 mm or larger, repeat colonoscopy in 6 months.

frontHtml: Link Barrett metaplasia to its malignant outcome.
backHtml: Barrett esophagus (goblet-cell intestinal metaplasia) is the precursor of distal esophageal adenocarcinoma.

frontHtml: Identify the adhesion defect behind hereditary diffuse gastric cancer.
backHtml: Diffuse gastric cancer with lobular breast cancer in a family points to germline CDH1 (E-cadherin) loss.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of targeted therapy for GIST.
backHtml: GIST is KIT/PDGFRA-driven; imatinib inhibits that tyrosine kinase.

frontHtml: Connect microsatellite instability to its DNA repair defect.
backHtml: Microsatellite instability equals defective mismatch repair; germline loss is Lynch syndrome.

frontHtml: Explain the nutritional consequence of carcinoid syndrome.
backHtml: Carcinoid syndrome can cause pellagra because tryptophan is diverted from niacin synthesis to serotonin.

frontHtml: Relate a dietary carcinogen to its signature mutation.
backHtml: Aflatoxin causes HCC through a characteristic TP53 codon 249 transversion.

frontHtml: Describe the molecular defect of mutant KRAS in pancreatic cancer.
backHtml: KRAS, mutated in most pancreatic adenocarcinomas, is locked on because it fails to hydrolyse GTP.

frontHtml: Predict the histology of esophageal cancer from location and risk factors.
backHtml: Mid-esophageal cancer in a smoker and drinker is squamous cell carcinoma with keratinisation.

frontHtml: Identify the infectious cause of cholangiocarcinoma.
backHtml: Liver flukes from raw freshwater fish (Clonorchis, Opisthorchis) cause cholangiocarcinoma.

frontHtml: Apply current USPSTF colorectal screening recommendations.
backHtml: Average-risk colorectal cancer screening starts at age 45.

frontHtml: Choose the evaluation of iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult.
backHtml: Unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia in an older adult needs colonoscopy and upper endoscopy, not stool testing.

frontHtml: Choose the next test for a liver nodule found on HCC surveillance.
backHtml: A surveillance nodule of 1 cm or more in cirrhosis needs multiphase CT or MRI.

frontHtml: Apply noninvasive imaging criteria for HCC.
backHtml: In cirrhosis, arterial enhancement with washout on multiphase imaging diagnoses HCC without biopsy.

frontHtml: Select the initial imaging for suspected pancreatic head cancer.
backHtml: Suspected pancreatic cancer is evaluated first with pancreas-protocol CT, not a tumour marker.

frontHtml: Choose first-line therapy for gastric MALT lymphoma.
backHtml: Localised H. pylori-positive gastric MALT lymphoma is treated first by eradicating H. pylori.

frontHtml: Manage Barrett esophagus with high-grade dysplasia.
backHtml: Barrett esophagus with confirmed dysplasia is treated endoscopically, not with surveillance or esophagectomy.

frontHtml: Stage a newly diagnosed rectal cancer.
backHtml: Rectal cancer is locally staged with pelvic MRI after CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

frontHtml: Apply universal tumour screening for Lynch syndrome.
backHtml: Every colorectal cancer gets universal mismatch repair (or MSI) testing.

frontHtml: Explain the anatomic basis of hepatic metastasis from colorectal cancer.
backHtml: Portal venous drainage makes the liver the first stop for metastases from most of the GI tract.

frontHtml: Identify the usual primary of a Krukenberg tumour.
backHtml: Krukenberg tumour: bilateral signet-ring ovarian metastases, usually from the stomach.

frontHtml: Explain the anatomic basis of the left supraclavicular node sign.
backHtml: A Virchow node reflects abdominal lymph flowing up the thoracic duct to the left venous angle.

frontHtml: Recognise metastatic melanoma in the GI tract.
backHtml: Melanoma is the commonest metastasis to the small bowel and can present late with bleeding or intussusception.

frontHtml: Distinguish metastatic lobular breast cancer from primary diffuse gastric cancer.
backHtml: ER/GATA3-positive, E-cadherin-negative single-file cells in the stomach indicate metastatic lobular breast cancer.

frontHtml: Apply SAAG to the mechanism of malignant ascites.
backHtml: Peritoneal carcinomatosis causes low-SAAG, high-protein ascites through permeability and lymphatic obstruction.

frontHtml: Describe the biochemistry of basement membrane invasion.
backHtml: Invasion requires metalloproteinases that degrade basement membrane type IV collagen.

frontHtml: Recognise the characteristic adverse effect of oxaliplatin.
backHtml: Cold-triggered dysesthesias are characteristic of oxaliplatin.

frontHtml: Explain resistance to anti-EGFR antibodies in RAS-mutant colorectal cancer.
backHtml: Activating RAS mutations make EGFR antibodies useless because signalling is constitutive downstream.

frontHtml: Manage isolated colorectal liver metastases.
backHtml: Resectable liver-only colorectal metastases are treated with curative-intent resection.

frontHtml: Interpret a rising tumour marker during surveillance.
backHtml: A rising CEA after colorectal cancer resection calls for CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

frontHtml: Recognise physical signs of metastatic gastric cancer.
backHtml: Virchow node plus periumbilical nodule with early satiety indicates advanced gastric cancer.

frontHtml: Choose the staging study for a new colon cancer.
backHtml: Stage colorectal cancer with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis plus baseline CEA.

frontHtml: Counsel a patient requesting tumour markers for screening.
backHtml: Tumour markers are for follow-up, never for screening asymptomatic people.

frontHtml: Choose the first test for ascites in a patient with cancer.
backHtml: New ascites needs diagnostic paracentesis with SAAG, protein and cytology before treatment.

frontHtml: Palliate recurrent malignant ascites.
backHtml: Rapidly recurrent malignant ascites is palliated with a tunnelled indwelling peritoneal catheter.

frontHtml: Choose palliative pharmacotherapy for malignant bowel obstruction.
backHtml: Octreotide reduces secretions and vomiting in inoperable malignant bowel obstruction; avoid prokinetics.

frontHtml: Manage malignant biliary obstruction in metastatic disease.
backHtml: Jaundice with dilated ducts in metastatic pancreatic cancer is palliated with an endoscopic metal stent.

frontHtml: Link a chemotherapy antiemetic to its receptor and adverse effect.
backHtml: 5-HT3 antagonists such as ondansetron can prolong the QT interval.

frontHtml: Explain extrapyramidal effects of dopamine-blocking antiemetics.
backHtml: Acute dystonia from antiemetics reflects nigrostriatal D2 blockade.

frontHtml: Identify the NK1 antagonist antiemetic.
backHtml: NK1 antagonists (aprepitant) block substance P and target delayed chemotherapy nausea.

frontHtml: Recognise anticholinergic adverse effects of motion-sickness therapy.
backHtml: Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist with anticholinergic toxicity in older adults.

frontHtml: Explain how the chemoreceptor trigger zone detects emetogenic chemicals.
backHtml: The chemoreceptor trigger zone in the area postrema lies outside the blood-brain barrier.

frontHtml: Calculate and interpret the stool osmotic gap.
backHtml: A high stool osmotic gap that resolves with fasting means osmotic diarrhoea, such as lactase deficiency.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of a secretory diarrhoea toxin.
backHtml: Cholera toxin causes secretory diarrhoea by ADP-ribosylating Gs and raising cAMP.

frontHtml: Distinguish visceral from parietal abdominal pain.
backHtml: Early appendicitis pain is periumbilical because midgut visceral afferents enter at T10.

frontHtml: Explain the maintenance of metabolic alkalosis after vomiting.
backHtml: Vomiting alkalosis is maintained by volume contraction, chloride depletion and aldosterone.

frontHtml: Order appropriate testing for suspected IBS.
backHtml: Suspected IBS with diarrhoea needs celiac serology, not routine colonoscopy or CT.

frontHtml: Choose the evaluation of dyspepsia by age and alarm features.
backHtml: New dyspepsia at age 60 or older, especially with weight loss, needs upper endoscopy.

frontHtml: Localise GI bleeding using clinical and laboratory clues.
backHtml: Melena with a disproportionately raised BUN in an NSAID user suggests a bleeding peptic ulcer.

frontHtml: Manage suspected upper GI bleeding after resuscitation.
backHtml: Resuscitate, give an IV PPI and perform upper endoscopy within 24 hours for upper GI bleeding.

frontHtml: Correct fluid and electrolyte losses from prolonged vomiting.
backHtml: Vomiting-induced metabolic alkalosis is treated with normal saline plus potassium chloride.

frontHtml: Manage opioid-induced constipation in a patient with cancer pain.
backHtml: Refractory opioid-induced constipation is treated with a peripherally acting mu-opioid antagonist.

frontHtml: Manage dehydration from acute gastroenteritis in a child.
backHtml: Oral rehydration solution is first line for mild to moderate paediatric dehydration.

frontHtml: Select an antiemetic for a patient with Parkinson disease.
backHtml: In Parkinson disease use ondansetron and avoid dopamine-antagonist antiemetics.

frontHtml: Identify the organism responsible for oral hairy leukoplakia from its clinical and histologic features.
backHtml: Oral hairy leukoplakia is an EBV lesion of the lateral tongue that signals immunosuppression and is not a precancer.

frontHtml: Explain why pleomorphic adenoma recurs after simple enucleation.
backHtml: Pleomorphic adenoma recurs after enucleation because of tumor extensions beyond its incomplete capsule.

frontHtml: Recognize Warthin tumor from its epidemiology and cytology.
backHtml: Warthin tumor: older smoker, parotid tail, often bilateral, oncocytic epithelium over lymphoid stroma.

frontHtml: Relate drug-induced xerostomia to muscarinic M3 blockade.
backHtml: Antimuscarinic drugs cause dry mouth by blocking M3 receptors on salivary acinar cells.

frontHtml: Associate Behcet disease with its HLA type and clinical triad.
backHtml: Behcet disease: recurrent oral and genital ulcers, uveitis and pathergy, associated with HLA-B51.

frontHtml: Describe how fluoride prevents dental caries.
backHtml: Fluoride prevents caries mainly by forming acid-resistant fluorapatite and aiding remineralization.

frontHtml: Recognize the lymphoma risk in Sjogren syndrome.
backHtml: New persistent parotid enlargement in Sjogren syndrome suggests MALT lymphoma.

frontHtml: Explain the molecular basis of p16 positivity in HPV-related oropharyngeal carcinoma.
backHtml: p16 overexpression marks HPV-driven oropharyngeal cancer because E7 inactivates Rb.

frontHtml: Choose biopsy as the next step for a persistent red oral lesion in a high-risk patient.
backHtml: Persistent erythroplakia needs biopsy; it carries the highest malignant potential of oral lesions.

frontHtml: Prioritize airway management in Ludwig angina.
backHtml: In Ludwig angina with airway signs, secure the airway before imaging or anything else.

frontHtml: Select empiric antibiotic therapy for Ludwig angina.
backHtml: Treat Ludwig angina with IV antibiotics covering oral streptococci and anaerobes, such as ampicillin-sulbactam.

frontHtml: Manage acute bacterial parotitis and recognize its predisposing factors.
backHtml: Suppurative parotitis in a dehydrated older patient: rehydrate, stimulate saliva, and give IV anti-staphylococcal antibiotics.

frontHtml: Prevent oral candidiasis in patients using inhaled corticosteroids.
backHtml: Prevent inhaled-corticosteroid thrush by rinsing and spitting after each dose (and a spacer for metered-dose inhalers).

frontHtml: Choose fine-needle aspiration for a persistent cystic neck mass in an adult.
backHtml: Persistent adult neck mass: imaging and FNA, not more antibiotics or open biopsy first; think HPV-related oropharyngeal cancer.

frontHtml: Explain the neural basis of achalasia.
backHtml: Achalasia is caused by loss of NO/VIP inhibitory neurons in the myenteric plexus.

frontHtml: Identify the transmission route of Trypanosoma cruzi in Chagas-related achalasia.
backHtml: Chagas disease (T. cruzi, triatomine bug feces) causes secondary achalasia, megacolon and cardiomyopathy.

frontHtml: Predict manometric findings in systemic sclerosis.
backHtml: Scleroderma esophagus: hypotensive LES and absent distal peristalsis, causing severe reflux.

frontHtml: Identify the histology of Barrett esophagus.
backHtml: Barrett esophagus is intestinal metaplasia (columnar cells with goblet cells) of the distal esophagus.

frontHtml: Distinguish HSV from CMV and Candida esophagitis by endoscopy and histology.
backHtml: HSV esophagitis: small punched-out ulcers, multinucleated squamous cells with Cowdry A inclusions at the ulcer edge.

frontHtml: Describe the anatomy and mechanism of Zenker diverticulum.
backHtml: Zenker diverticulum is a false pulsion diverticulum through Killian triangle above the cricopharyngeus.

frontHtml: Recognize drugs that cause pill esophagitis.
backHtml: Doxycycline taken with little water before lying down is a classic cause of pill esophagitis.

frontHtml: Link Plummer-Vinson syndrome to iron deficiency.
backHtml: Plummer-Vinson syndrome: iron deficiency anemia, postcricoid web, dysphagia; treat the iron deficiency and watch for squamous cancer.

frontHtml: Identify the portosystemic anastomosis that forms esophageal varices.
backHtml: Esophageal varices form at the left gastric to azygos portosystemic anastomosis.

frontHtml: Start empiric PPI therapy for typical reflux without alarm features.
backHtml: Uncomplicated typical GERD: 8-week once-daily PPI trial before breakfast, plus lifestyle measures.

frontHtml: Choose manometry to confirm suspected achalasia.
backHtml: After endoscopy excludes obstruction, high-resolution manometry confirms achalasia.

frontHtml: Select definitive therapy for achalasia in a fit patient.
backHtml: Fit patients with achalasia get myotomy (Heller or POEM) or pneumatic dilation; botulinum toxin is for poor candidates.

frontHtml: Choose primary prophylaxis for large esophageal varices in compensated cirrhosis.
backHtml: Primary prophylaxis of large varices: nonselective beta blocker (carvedilol preferred) or band ligation if beta blockers cannot be used.

frontHtml: Distinguish Mallory-Weiss tear from Boerhaave syndrome and variceal bleeding.
backHtml: Retching then a small hematemesis in a stable patient suggests Mallory-Weiss; chest pain and crepitus suggest Boerhaave.

frontHtml: Manage suspected Candida esophagitis in HIV.
backHtml: Thrush plus odynophagia in advanced HIV: empiric oral fluconazole; endoscope only if no response.

frontHtml: Choose the surveillance interval for nondysplastic Barrett esophagus.
backHtml: Nondysplastic Barrett of 3 cm or more: PPI plus surveillance endoscopy every 3 years.

frontHtml: Choose the initial test for suspected Zenker diverticulum.
backHtml: Suspected Zenker diverticulum: barium swallow first, not blind endoscopy.

frontHtml: Describe the second messenger pathways that control parietal cell acid secretion.
backHtml: Histamine stimulates acid through H2 receptors, Gs and cAMP; gastrin and ACh act through Gq and calcium.

frontHtml: Predict the gastrin level and related findings in autoimmune atrophic gastritis.
backHtml: Autoimmune gastritis: achlorhydria, high gastrin, low pepsinogen I and B12 deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism and key adverse effects of misoprostol.
backHtml: Misoprostol is a PGE1 analog that replaces the mucosal protection NSAIDs remove; avoid in pregnancy.

frontHtml: Recognize hypomagnesemia as an adverse effect of long-term PPI therapy.
backHtml: Long-term PPIs can cause hypomagnesemia, which leads to hypocalcemia and hypokalemia.

frontHtml: Identify the histology of Menetrier disease and contrast it with Zollinger-Ellison syndrome.
backHtml: Menetrier disease: giant folds from foveolar hyperplasia, low acid and protein-losing gastropathy.

frontHtml: Distinguish the mechanisms of Cushing and Curling stress ulcers.
backHtml: Cushing ulcer (brain injury) = vagal acid hypersecretion; Curling ulcer (burns) = hypovolemic ischemia.

frontHtml: Relate ulcer location to the artery at risk of bleeding.
backHtml: Posterior duodenal ulcers bleed from the gastroduodenal artery; anterior ones perforate.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of metoclopramide-induced tardive dyskinesia.
backHtml: Metoclopramide blocks D2 receptors; long-term use can cause tardive dyskinesia.

frontHtml: Choose the timing of endoscopy in acute upper GI bleeding.
backHtml: Nonvariceal upper GI bleeding: resuscitate, start PPI, and perform endoscopy within 24 hours.

frontHtml: Match endoscopic ulcer stigmata to treatment.
backHtml: Active bleeding or a nonbleeding visible vessel needs endoscopic hemostasis followed by high-dose PPI.

frontHtml: Apply a restrictive transfusion threshold in upper GI bleeding.
backHtml: Stable upper GI bleeding without heart disease: transfuse only when hemoglobin falls below 7 g/dL.

frontHtml: Plan an appropriate test of cure after H. pylori treatment.
backHtml: Confirm H. pylori eradication in everyone, at least 4 weeks after treatment and 2 weeks off PPI, with a breath or stool test.

frontHtml: Choose the initial evaluation for uncomplicated dyspepsia in a younger adult.
backHtml: Dyspepsia under age 60 without alarm features: test and treat for H. pylori.

frontHtml: Choose the diagnostic test for suspected diabetic gastroparesis.
backHtml: Suspected gastroparesis: exclude obstruction with endoscopy, then confirm with 4-hour solid-meal scintigraphy.

frontHtml: Manage a perforated peptic ulcer.
backHtml: Perforated peptic ulcer with peritonitis needs resuscitation, antibiotics and emergency surgical repair.

frontHtml: Distinguish osmotic diarrhea due to lactase nonpersistence from secretory causes.
backHtml: Diarrhea that stops with fasting and a positive lactose hydrogen breath test indicate osmotic diarrhea from lactase deficiency.

frontHtml: Explain the cobalamin and folate pattern produced by bacterial overgrowth.
backHtml: Low B12 with high folate in a patient with stasis suggests small intestinal bacterial overgrowth.

frontHtml: Relate the duodenal site of iron absorption to iron deficiency after bariatric surgery.
backHtml: Iron is absorbed in the duodenum, so bypass operations that exclude it commonly cause refractory iron deficiency.

frontHtml: Identify the arterial watershed responsible for splenic flexure ischemia.
backHtml: Low-flow ischemic colitis targets watershed segments: the splenic flexure (SMA/IMA) and the rectosigmoid junction (IMA/internal iliac).

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of bile acid diarrhea after limited ileal resection.
backHtml: Short ileal loss causes secretory bile acid diarrhea that responds to sequestrants; long ileal loss causes steatorrhea.

frontHtml: Explain the link between aortic stenosis and bleeding from angiodysplasia.
backHtml: Aortic stenosis with bleeding cecal angiodysplasia (Heyde syndrome) reflects acquired loss of large vWF multimers from shear stress.

frontHtml: Choose the best initial test for suspected acute arterial mesenteric ischemia.
backHtml: Suspected acute mesenteric ischemia calls for immediate CT angiography; normal or mildly raised lactate must never delay it.

frontHtml: Manage complicated diverticulitis with a large abscess.
backHtml: A large diverticular abscess in a stable patient is drained percutaneously alongside IV antibiotics.

frontHtml: Plan follow-up evaluation after complicated diverticulitis.
backHtml: Perform colonoscopy after recovery from complicated diverticulitis when no recent examination exists.

frontHtml: Manage sigmoid volvulus without peritonitis.
backHtml: Uncomplicated sigmoid volvulus: endoscopic detorsion first, then elective sigmoid resection before discharge in fit patients.

frontHtml: Escalate management of acute colonic pseudo-obstruction after failed conservative care.
backHtml: Ogilvie syndrome that persists after 24 to 48 hours of conservative care, with a dilated cecum and no peritonitis, is treated with IV neostigmine.

frontHtml: Select imaging for suspected appendicitis in a pregnant patient.
backHtml: In pregnancy, image suspected appendicitis with ultrasound first, then noncontrast MRI if needed.

frontHtml: Relate the innervation of the anal canal to pain from hemorrhoids.
backHtml: Lesions above the pectinate line are painless (visceral innervation); lesions below it are painful (somatic pudendal innervation).

frontHtml: Predict lymphatic spread of a tumour below the pectinate line.
backHtml: Below the pectinate line, lymph drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

frontHtml: Identify the portosystemic anastomosis that forms anorectal varices.
backHtml: Anorectal varices form between the portal superior rectal vein and the systemic middle and inferior rectal veins.

frontHtml: Link the embryologic origin of the anorectum to its epithelium and tumour type.
backHtml: Above the pectinate line: endoderm, columnar epithelium, adenocarcinoma. Below: ectoderm, squamous epithelium, SCC.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of topical nitrate therapy for anal fissure.
backHtml: Topical nitrates heal fissures by NO-cGMP relaxation of the internal sphincter; headache is the typical adverse effect.

frontHtml: State the mechanism of botulinum toxin.
backHtml: Botulinum toxin cleaves SNARE proteins and blocks acetylcholine release, giving reversible sphincter relaxation.

frontHtml: Identify the microbiology of lymphogranuloma venereum proctitis.
backHtml: LGV proctitis is caused by C. trachomatis serovars L1 to L3, obligate intracellular bacteria with an elementary and a reticulate body.

frontHtml: Identify the HPV oncoprotein that inactivates Rb.
backHtml: HPV E7 inactivates Rb; E6 degrades p53.

frontHtml: Localise the nerve responsible for external anal sphincter weakness.
backHtml: Reduced squeeze pressure with intact sphincters after a difficult delivery suggests pudendal nerve injury.

frontHtml: Manage an acutely thrombosed external hemorrhoid.
backHtml: Thrombosed external hemorrhoid seen within about 72 hours: excise under local anesthesia; later, treat conservatively.

frontHtml: Recognise an atypical anal fissure and evaluate for a secondary cause.
backHtml: An off-midline anal fissure demands a search for Crohn disease, HIV, TB, syphilis or cancer before fissure-directed treatment.

frontHtml: Choose empiric treatment for sexually transmitted proctitis.
backHtml: Empiric treatment for STI proctitis is ceftriaxone plus doxycycline, extended to 21 days of doxycycline when LGV is suspected.

frontHtml: Manage an acute perianal abscess.
backHtml: Anorectal abscess: drain it; antibiotics are an adjunct for cellulitis, systemic illness, diabetes or immunosuppression.

frontHtml: Treat a simple low anal fistula after abscess drainage.
backHtml: Simple low anal fistula: fistulotomy. Complex or high fistula: seton and sphincter-sparing techniques.

frontHtml: Choose initial therapy for locoregional anal squamous cell carcinoma.
backHtml: Anal SCC is treated with chemoradiation (5-FU or capecitabine plus mitomycin); surgery is salvage.

frontHtml: Select local staging imaging for rectal adenocarcinoma.
backHtml: Use pelvic MRI for local staging of rectal cancer; CT chest, abdomen and pelvis and CEA complete staging.

frontHtml: Distinguish full-thickness rectal prolapse from other protruding anal lesions.
backHtml: Concentric folds mean full-thickness rectal prolapse; radial folds mean hemorrhoids or mucosal prolapse.

frontHtml: Distinguish Crigler-Najjar type I from other inherited hyperbilirubinemias.
backHtml: Crigler-Najjar type I is absent UGT1A1 activity: severe neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that phenobarbital cannot lower.

frontHtml: Identify the transporter defect in Dubin-Johnson syndrome.
backHtml: Conjugated hyperbilirubinemia with normal enzymes and a black liver is Dubin-Johnson syndrome (MRP2 defect).

frontHtml: Identify the gene product defective in Wilson disease.
backHtml: Wilson disease is an ATP7B defect: impaired biliary copper excretion and ceruloplasmin loading.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of liver injury in alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.
backHtml: In alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, liver disease comes from retained misfolded protein; lung disease comes from lack of circulating inhibitor.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of lactulose in hepatic encephalopathy.
backHtml: Lactulose lowers blood ammonia by colonic acidification (NH3 trapped as NH4+) and catharsis.

frontHtml: Recognise the composition of Mallory-Denk bodies in alcohol-associated hepatitis.
backHtml: Mallory-Denk bodies are ubiquitinated keratin intermediate filament aggregates, typical of alcohol-associated hepatitis.

frontHtml: Calculate severity and choose therapy for severe alcohol-associated hepatitis.
backHtml: Severe alcohol-associated hepatitis (Maddrey 32 or more, or MELD above 20) without infection or bleeding is treated with prednisolone, reassessed by the Lille score at day 7.

frontHtml: Risk-stratify fibrosis in a patient with MASLD.
backHtml: In MASLD, risk-stratify fibrosis with FIB-4 first, then elastography if FIB-4 is not low.

frontHtml: Screen first-degree relatives for HFE hemochromatosis.
backHtml: Screen first-degree relatives of a C282Y homozygote with transferrin saturation, ferritin and HFE genotyping.

frontHtml: Choose the initial imaging study for suspected Budd-Chiari syndrome.
backHtml: Suspected Budd-Chiari syndrome is evaluated first with Doppler ultrasonography of the hepatic veins.

frontHtml: Recognise Wilson disease presenting as acute liver failure.
backHtml: Acute liver failure in a young patient with Coombs-negative hemolysis and a very low alkaline phosphatase suggests Wilson disease.

frontHtml: Manage Wilson disease presenting as acute liver failure.
backHtml: Fulminant Wilson disease requires urgent liver transplantation; chelation is for chronic disease.

frontHtml: Explain why rapid weight loss predisposes to cholesterol gallstones.
backHtml: Rapid weight loss causes cholesterol stones through cholesterol supersaturation and gallbladder hypomotility.

frontHtml: Identify the gallstone type produced by chronic hemolysis.
backHtml: Chronic hemolysis causes black pigment (calcium bilirubinate) gallstones, often radiopaque.

frontHtml: Describe the mechanism of brown pigment stone formation.
backHtml: Brown pigment stones form in infected ducts when bacterial β-glucuronidase deconjugates bilirubin.

frontHtml: Identify the target antigen of the antimitochondrial antibody in PBC.
backHtml: Antimitochondrial antibodies in PBC target the E2 subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

frontHtml: Recognize the histology of primary sclerosing cholangitis.
backHtml: PSC shows onion-skin periductal fibrosis and is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis.

frontHtml: Explain how fibrates predispose to cholesterol gallstones.
backHtml: Fibrates cause cholesterol gallstones by inhibiting 7α-hydroxylase and raising biliary cholesterol.

frontHtml: Identify the source and actions of cholecystokinin.
backHtml: CCK from duodenal and jejunal I cells contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi.

frontHtml: Describe the proposed pathogenesis of choledochal cysts.
backHtml: Choledochal cysts are linked to an anomalous pancreaticobiliary junction that lets pancreatic juice reflux into the bile duct.

frontHtml: Explain the pathogenesis of gallstone ileus.
backHtml: Gallstone ileus: a large stone enters the duodenum through a cholecystoenteric fistula and impacts at the terminal ileum.

frontHtml: Choose ERCP for a high-likelihood common bile duct stone.
backHtml: When ultrasound shows a common bile duct stone, go straight to ERCP for removal, then cholecystectomy.

frontHtml: Diagnose acalculous cholecystitis in a critically ill patient.
backHtml: A febrile ICU patient with a thick-walled, distended gallbladder and no stones has acalculous cholecystitis until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: Select percutaneous cholecystostomy for an unstable patient with cholecystitis.
backHtml: Unstable patients with acute cholecystitis, especially acalculous disease in the ICU, are treated with percutaneous cholecystostomy.

frontHtml: Choose MRCP to diagnose primary sclerosing cholangitis.
backHtml: Suspected PSC is diagnosed with MRCP; ERCP is reserved for treatment or tissue sampling.

frontHtml: Select first-line therapy for primary biliary cholangitis.
backHtml: Ursodeoxycholic acid is first-line, lifelong therapy for primary biliary cholangitis.

frontHtml: Manage acute cholecystitis during pregnancy.
backHtml: Acute cholecystitis in pregnancy is treated with laparoscopic cholecystectomy during the admission, in any trimester.

frontHtml: Describe the action of secretin on the exocrine pancreas.
backHtml: Secretin, released by duodenal acid, stimulates bicarbonate-rich fluid from pancreatic ductal cells.

frontHtml: Explain the role of enteropeptidase in protease activation.
backHtml: Enteropeptidase activates trypsinogen, which then activates the other pancreatic zymogens.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of PRSS1-related hereditary pancreatitis.
backHtml: PRSS1 gain-of-function variants cause autosomal dominant hereditary pancreatitis by leaving activated trypsin uncontrolled.

frontHtml: Recognize familial chylomicronemia as a cause of pancreatitis.
backHtml: Lipoprotein lipase deficiency causes chylomicronemia, eruptive xanthomas and recurrent pancreatitis in childhood.

frontHtml: Recognize the histology of IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis.
backHtml: IgG4-related autoimmune pancreatitis shows IgG4-rich lymphoplasmacytic inflammation, storiform fibrosis and obliterative phlebitis.

frontHtml: Describe the histology of a pancreatic pseudocyst.
backHtml: Pancreatic pseudocysts are walled by fibrous and granulation tissue and lack an epithelial lining.

frontHtml: Explain why exocrine pancreatic insufficiency can cause B12 deficiency.
backHtml: Pancreatic proteases free B12 from haptocorrin; exocrine insufficiency can therefore impair B12 absorption.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of pancreatic insufficiency in cystic fibrosis.
backHtml: Cystic fibrosis causes pancreatic insufficiency because thick ductal secretions obstruct the ducts and destroy acini.

frontHtml: Choose initial fluid therapy for acute pancreatitis.
backHtml: Initial treatment of acute pancreatitis is moderate goal-directed lactated Ringer solution with frequent reassessment.

frontHtml: Identify hypertriglyceridemia as a cause of acute pancreatitis.
backHtml: Lipemic serum with acute pancreatitis suggests hypertriglyceridemia; measure triglycerides early.

frontHtml: Plan secondary prevention after hypertriglyceridemia-induced pancreatitis.
backHtml: Prevent recurrent hypertriglyceridemic pancreatitis with a fibrate, dietary fat restriction and glucose control.

frontHtml: Manage an asymptomatic pancreatic pseudocyst.
backHtml: Asymptomatic pancreatic pseudocysts are observed; size alone is not an indication to drain.

frontHtml: Manage infected pancreatic necrosis.
backHtml: Infected pancreatic necrosis in a stable patient: carbapenem first, then delayed, step-up drainage of walled-off necrosis.

frontHtml: Treat exocrine insufficiency in chronic pancreatitis.
backHtml: Steatorrhea from chronic pancreatitis is treated with pancreatic enzyme replacement taken with meals.

frontHtml: Select prophylaxis against post-ERCP pancreatitis.
backHtml: Rectal NSAIDs (indomethacin or diclofenac) at the time of ERCP reduce post-ERCP pancreatitis.

frontHtml: Relate SAAG to Starling forces in cirrhotic ascites.
backHtml: A SAAG of 1.1 g/dL or more reflects raised portal (sinusoidal) hydrostatic pressure as the cause of ascites.

frontHtml: Explain the role of splanchnic vasodilation in cirrhotic ascites.
backHtml: Splanchnic vasodilation from nitric oxide underlies the RAAS activation and sodium retention of cirrhosis.

frontHtml: Identify the mechanism of spironolactone-induced gynecomastia.
backHtml: Spironolactone causes gynecomastia through androgen receptor antagonism; switch to eplerenone or amiloride if needed.

frontHtml: Identify the usual organisms in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
backHtml: SBP is typically a single enteric gram-negative organism, most often E. coli .

frontHtml: Describe the pathophysiology of hepatorenal syndrome.
backHtml: Hepatorenal syndrome is functional renal vasoconstriction in structurally normal kidneys, with very low urine sodium.

frontHtml: Recognize the causes of chylous ascites.
backHtml: Chylous ascites (triglycerides above 200 mg/dL) in an adult with bulky nodes suggests lymphoma.

frontHtml: Associate peritoneal mesothelioma with asbestos.
backHtml: Malignant mesothelioma, pleural or peritoneal, is strongly associated with asbestos exposure.

frontHtml: Recognize the pathology of tuberculous peritonitis.
backHtml: Tuberculous peritonitis: lymphocytic, high-protein, low-SAAG ascites; peritoneal biopsy shows caseating granulomas.

frontHtml: Treat spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with antibiotics and albumin.
backHtml: SBP (ascitic PMN of 250/mm3 or more): give an IV third-generation cephalosporin plus IV albumin.

frontHtml: Recognize secondary bacterial peritonitis in a patient with ascites.
backHtml: Polymicrobial ascites with low glucose and high LDH means secondary peritonitis: broad antibiotics and urgent CT for a source.

frontHtml: Manage secondary peritonitis from a perforated viscus.
backHtml: Secondary peritonitis from a free perforation needs surgical source control along with antibiotics.

frontHtml: Use SAAG and ascitic protein to identify cardiac ascites.
backHtml: High SAAG with high ascitic protein (2.5 g/dL or more) suggests cardiac ascites or hepatic vein obstruction.

frontHtml: Prevent post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction with albumin.
backHtml: After large-volume paracentesis (more than 5 L), give IV albumin, about 6 to 8 g per liter removed.

frontHtml: Start first-line treatment for cirrhotic ascites.
backHtml: Initial treatment of cirrhotic ascites is about 2 g/day sodium restriction plus spironolactone and furosemide.

frontHtml: Treat hepatorenal syndrome.
backHtml: Treat hepatorenal syndrome with a vasoconstrictor (terlipressin, or norepinephrine in the ICU) plus albumin.

frontHtml: Provide secondary prophylaxis after spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
backHtml: After a first episode of SBP, give long-term daily oral antibiotic prophylaxis and refer for transplant evaluation.

frontHtml: Relate an indirect inguinal hernia to failed obliteration of the processus vaginalis.
backHtml: Indirect inguinal hernia equals a patent processus vaginalis entering lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

frontHtml: Identify the boundaries of Hesselbach triangle.
backHtml: Direct hernias bulge medial to the inferior epigastric vessels through Hesselbach triangle.

frontHtml: Locate the femoral canal and its relations.
backHtml: A femoral hernia lies below the inguinal ligament, immediately medial to the femoral vein.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of late dumping syndrome.
backHtml: Postprandial hypoglycemia hours after gastric surgery is late dumping from an insulin overshoot.

frontHtml: Explain B12 deficiency in blind loop syndrome.
backHtml: Low B12 with high folate after a blind loop suggests bacterial overgrowth.

frontHtml: Link nutrient deficiency after bariatric surgery to its absorption site.
backHtml: Iron deficiency after gastric bypass reflects duodenal bypass and reduced acid.

frontHtml: Distinguish Boerhaave rupture from other esophageal lesions.
backHtml: Vomiting followed by chest pain and subcutaneous emphysema means transmural rupture, not a Mallory-Weiss tear.

frontHtml: Relate duodenal retroperitoneal anatomy to its injury mechanism.
backHtml: A handlebar injury with delayed bilious vomiting suggests a duodenal hematoma.

frontHtml: Choose the confirmatory study for suspected esophageal perforation.
backHtml: Suspected esophageal perforation is confirmed with water-soluble contrast esophagography or CT with oral contrast.

frontHtml: Manage confirmed spontaneous esophageal rupture.
backHtml: Boerhaave rupture with free contamination needs emergent surgical repair plus drainage.

frontHtml: Apply the FAST and stability algorithm in blunt abdominal trauma.
backHtml: Unstable plus positive FAST after blunt trauma means laparotomy.

frontHtml: Recognize indications for laparotomy after penetrating abdominal trauma.
backHtml: Evisceration after an abdominal stab wound is an indication for laparotomy even when the patient is stable.

frontHtml: Manage ingestion of a button battery lodged in the esophagus.
backHtml: An esophageal button battery requires emergent endoscopic removal.

frontHtml: Manage early dumping syndrome after bariatric surgery.
backHtml: Early dumping is treated first with dietary modification.

frontHtml: Explain the embryologic basis of omphalocele.
backHtml: Omphalocele is a membrane-covered midline defect from failure of the physiologically herniated gut to return.

frontHtml: Identify the type of esophageal atresia from radiographic findings.
backHtml: Coiled tube plus gas in the abdomen means proximal atresia with a distal tracheesophageal fistula.

frontHtml: Explain the embryologic origin of annular pancreas.
backHtml: Annular pancreas comes from abnormal migration of the ventral pancreatic bud around the duodenum.

frontHtml: Relate Meckel diverticulum to its embryologic origin.
backHtml: Meckel diverticulum is a vitelline duct remnant; ectopic gastric mucosa causes bleeding and a positive pertechnetate scan.

frontHtml: Identify the embryologic basis of cleft lip.
backHtml: Cleft lip is failed fusion of the maxillary prominence with the medial nasal prominences.

frontHtml: Explain the acid-base and renal response in pyloric stenosis.
backHtml: Paradoxical aciduria in pyloric stenosis reflects volume-driven aldosterone action plus chloride depletion.

frontHtml: Choose the best imaging test for suspected pyloric stenosis.
backHtml: Suspected pyloric stenosis is confirmed by abdominal ultrasound.

frontHtml: Sequence management of pyloric stenosis.
backHtml: In pyloric stenosis, correct fluids and electrolytes first; pyloromyotomy follows.

frontHtml: Manage biliary atresia.
backHtml: Biliary atresia is treated with an early Kasai procedure; delay worsens outcomes.

frontHtml: Manage duodenal atresia in a newborn.
backHtml: Duodenal atresia is managed with decompression, fluids and duodenoduodenostomy.

frontHtml: Evaluate a newborn with omphalocele for associated anomalies.
backHtml: Omphalocele demands a search for associated anomalies, starting with echocardiography.

frontHtml: Choose the diagnostic test for suspected Meckel diverticulum.
backHtml: Painless lower GI bleeding in a toddler calls for a Meckel (pertechnetate) scan.

frontHtml: Explain how NSAIDs cause peptic ulcers.
backHtml: NSAID ulcers result mainly from loss of COX-1-derived mucosal prostaglandins.

frontHtml: Explain the zonal pattern of acetaminophen hepatotoxicity.
backHtml: Acetaminophen causes zone 3 necrosis because CYP2E1 is concentrated there.

frontHtml: Recognize the main adverse effect of misoprostol.
backHtml: Misoprostol prevents NSAID ulcers but commonly causes diarrhea.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of peripherally acting opioid antagonists.
backHtml: PAMORAs relieve opioid constipation because they block gut mu receptors but stay out of the brain.

frontHtml: Classify drug-induced liver injury and link it to amoxicillin-clavulanate.
backHtml: Delayed cholestatic jaundice after amoxicillin-clavulanate is classic idiosyncratic DILI.

frontHtml: Explain the mechanism of immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis.
backHtml: Checkpoint-inhibitor colitis is autoimmune T-cell injury from loss of inhibitory checkpoints.

frontHtml: Choose the diagnostic test for suspected C. difficile infection.
backHtml: Test unformed stool for C. difficile when diarrhea follows antibiotics.

frontHtml: Select therapy for an initial C. difficile infection.
backHtml: Treat a first C. difficile episode with oral fidaxomicin (or oral vancomycin).

frontHtml: Use the Rumack-Matthew nomogram to decide on N-acetylcysteine.
backHtml: A post-4-hour acetaminophen level above the treatment line means start NAC immediately.

frontHtml: Prevent NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease in high-risk patients.
backHtml: High-GI-risk patients who need an NSAID should receive a PPI.

frontHtml: Manage laxative-refractory opioid-induced constipation.
backHtml: Laxative-refractory opioid constipation calls for a PAMORA once obstruction is excluded.

frontHtml: Recognize and manage drug-induced pancreatitis.
backHtml: Thiopurine-induced pancreatitis requires stopping the drug class permanently.

frontHtml: Manage immune checkpoint inhibitor colitis.
backHtml: Moderate to severe checkpoint-inhibitor colitis is treated by holding the drug and giving glucocorticoids.

frontHtml: Apply stopping rules for isoniazid hepatotoxicity.
backHtml: Symptomatic isoniazid hepatitis with ALT above 3 times normal requires stopping isoniazid.
